explanation:
### The design

```systemverilog
localparam int AW = $clog2(DEPTH);
logic [AW-1:0] wptr, rptr;
logic [AW:0]   count;            // one bit wider: 0 .. DEPTH is DEPTH+1 values

assign empty = (count == '0);
assign full  = (count == DEPTH[AW:0]);

wire take_w = wr_en && !full;
wire take_r = rd_en && !empty;

fifo_mem #(.WIDTH(WIDTH), .DEPTH(DEPTH)) store (
    .clk(clk), .we(take_w), .waddr(wptr), .wdata(wdata),
    .raddr(rptr), .rdata(rdata)
);

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (rst) begin
        wptr <= '0; rptr <= '0; count <= '0;
    end else begin
        if (take_w) wptr <= wptr + 1'b1;
        if (take_r) rptr <= rptr + 1'b1;
        if      (take_w && !take_r) count <= count + 1'b1;
        else if (take_r && !take_w) count <= count - 1'b1;
    end
end
```

### The off-by-one that is not an off-by-one

`count` is one bit wider than the pointers. A depth-8 FIFO holds 0, 1, … 8
items, which is nine values and needs four bits; the pointers only need three,
because they index 0 … 7 and wrap. Declaring `count` the same width as the
pointers makes `count == DEPTH` unreachable — it wraps to zero instead — so
`full` is never true and the FIFO silently overwrites itself. That is the
classic version of this bug, and it passes a test that never fills the thing.

### Why a count at all

Two pointers are enough to address the memory and not enough to describe the
state. When `wptr == rptr` the FIFO is either completely empty or completely
full, and the pointers cannot tell you which. There are three standard fixes:

1. **A count**, as above. Costs a small adder and answers directly.
2. **An extra bit on each pointer.** Equal pointers with equal top bits is
   empty; equal pointers with different top bits is full. Costs two flip-flops
   and no adder, and is what a clock-crossing FIFO uses, because a count that
   two clock domains both update cannot be synchronised and pointers can.
3. **Keep one slot empty.** `full` is "the write pointer is one behind the
   read pointer". Costs a slot of capacity, which on a depth of four is a
   quarter of the thing.

### Why `take_w` and `take_r` are computed first

The rule in the statement is that a write while full is refused *even if a
read happens on the same edge*. Working both decisions out from the state as
it is now, before anything moves, is what makes that true. Deciding the write
after applying the read — "there is room now, so take it" — is a defensible
FIFO and a different one, and it is the version that makes a simultaneous
read and write at full succeed. Either can be built; the specification says
which this one is, and the grading testbench checks it.

### Where the read latency comes from

`raddr` is driven by `rptr` **as it is now**, not by `rptr + 1`. On the edge
that takes a read, the memory captures `store[rptr]` — the oldest item — and
`rptr` moves on. So the item appears on `rdata` in the cycle after that edge,
which is exactly the one-cycle latency milestone 1 built. The two modules fit
together because both were specified around the same edge.
